title: The Fed's Preferred Inflation Gauge Is About to Print 3.8 Per Cent. Oil Is Back Above $94. Your Mortgage Rate Is Not Coming Down.
excerpt: Today's PCE data will confirm what markets already fear: the Hormuz crisis has embedded itself in American prices. Here is what it means for NRI homebuyers, remittances, and summer trips to India.
body:
The Bureau of Economic Analysis will release the April Personal Consumption Expenditures price index at 8:30 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, and economists are not expecting good news. The consensus forecast, surveyed by FactSet, puts headline PCE inflation at 3.8 to 3.9 per cent year over year — the highest reading since May 2023 and a sharp acceleration from March's 3.5 per cent.

Core PCE, which strips out food and energy and is the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of underlying price pressures, is expected to tick up to 3.3 per cent from 3.2 per cent in March.

This is the first major inflation report in the Kevin Warsh era at the Fed, and it will land on a market already rattled by fresh US military strikes against Iran overnight.

The Oil Connection

Brent crude futures climbed about 2 per cent on Thursday morning to trade around $94 a barrel, partially reversing Wednesday's sharp 5.3 per cent decline. That decline had come on reports of a draft US-Iran framework that included restoring commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz within a month. But overnight strikes from both sides have tested the fragile ceasefire, and traders are recalibrating.

The Iran war-driven energy shock has been the single largest driver of the inflation reacceleration. Jet fuel prices in India have surged from ₹80,000 to over ₹1 lakh per kilolitre, forcing Air India to cut 22 per cent of its domestic flights between June and August. IndiGo is trimming 5 to 7 per cent. If you have booked internal flights in India for this summer, check your itinerary.

What It Means for Mortgage Rates

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate stood at 6.62 per cent as of Tuesday, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is down from recent highs but still punishing for anyone trying to buy a home in the Bay Area, New Jersey, or the other metros where Indian Americans concentrate.

Minutes from the Fed's April meeting, released last Wednesday, revealed that officials discussed the possibility of raising the federal-funds rate if inflation remains elevated. Markets are pricing in roughly a 50 per cent probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike by year-end.

If the Fed hikes, mortgage rates will follow. The window for rate relief that many NRI homebuyers were waiting for has effectively closed for 2026.

The Dollar-Rupee Equation

The rupee slipped to 95.69 against the dollar on Wednesday as Indian equities fell on news of fresh US strikes on Iran. The RBI conducted a $5 billion dollar-rupee buy-sell swap on Tuesday that was nearly twice oversubscribed — receiving $9.8 billion in bids — a sign of how aggressively the central bank is trying to manage dollar demand.

For NRIs sending money home, the strong dollar is a silver lining. Every dollar converts to more rupees, making remittances more valuable. But the same dynamic that strengthens the dollar — persistent US inflation, high interest rates, geopolitical risk — is also what makes everything in America more expensive.

India's Markets: A Stock-Picker's June

Indian markets will be closed on Thursday for a local holiday, but the picture heading into June is clear. The Nifty 50 ended the May derivatives series little changed at 23,913.7 points. Foreign investors have pulled out $24.3 billion from Indian equities so far in 2026, surpassing last year's record annual outflows. Taiwan, buoyed by TSMC's AI surge, has overtaken India as the world's fifth-largest stock market.

Two brokerages told Reuters this week that India is on track to become a stock-picker's market in June — meaning broad index gains will be limited, but selective sectors could outperform. Metal stocks rallied on the Quad nations' critical minerals framework. HDFC Bank dragged.

For NRI investors with India exposure through mutual funds or direct equity, the message is: do not expect the index to do the work. Sector selection matters more than it has in years.

The Summer Squeeze

The practical impact of all these forces converges on one question many NRI families are asking right now: can we afford to go to India this summer?

US-India airfares have surged. Airlines are warning of sky-high fares through August. Air India has already cut 27 per cent of international routes. Delhi and Maharashtra have cut VAT on aviation turbine fuel to 7 per cent each to ease pressure, but the savings have not yet flowed through to ticket prices.

Add in the heatwave that has killed at least 77 people in India, the domestic flight cuts, and hotel prices that have not adjusted downward, and the calculus has shifted. Some families are delaying trips to September or October, when fares historically drop and the monsoon breaks the heat.

What to Watch

The PCE number drops at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. If it comes in at or above 3.9 per cent, expect Treasury yields to rise, stock futures to wobble, and the conversation about a Fed rate hike to intensify. If it surprises to the downside — unlikely, but possible — there may be a brief rally.

Either way, the structural picture has not changed: oil above $90, inflation above 3.5 per cent, the Fed on hold or hawkish, and the Hormuz crisis unresolved. Plan accordingly.
